en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the burden of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and the gloss on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*), Oṃ Śrī Śrīnivāsa Svāmin.
Oṃ Śrī Vināyaka Svāmin,
Oṃ Śrī Sarasvatī Devī; now begins the recitation known as the Atideśapārāyaṇa.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
The declaration of the subject matter of this treatise:

An answer is now stated for those who do not accept the extended application (*atideśa*) of ritual elements (*padārtha*) to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), nor the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding its specific form (*prakāra*). (1)

The presentation of one's own established doctrine: "By means of the original benefit, by the primary objects, and by the modified ones, as well as by its own performance-injunction, the injunction is said to be connected. (Verse 2)
Whatever is desired and appropriate presents itself as proximate;
indeed, the meaning of the injunction is described by its own word as being accompanied by that very thing. (3)
And the meaning of the injunction, being that which is to be accomplished, requires an auxiliary;
and that [auxiliary], being suitable, is brought into proximity by means of the sentence and other factors, as well as by the archetypal rule (*prakṛti*).

Even though this archetypal assistance is preceded by its constituent parts, it is brought into proximity within the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) because it cannot otherwise be understood [as applicable].
Nevertheless, because it requires them, an injunction first adopts the mode [of action],
while it disregards the objects already understood through other means.
But later, when those [causes] are again required for the sake of accomplishing the benefit,
and are obtained by virtue of that [result], it attains its continuity.
In every case, it is held that there is a connection by way of the relationship between the primary and the subordinate;
and the injunction is considered the primary element, while the ritual properties are regarded as subordinate to it.
Furthermore, there is no denotation of that which is already connected [with another word],
because in rites such as the Pitṛyajña, it is observed that the connection occurs even with an agent who is merely to be inferred through the words present in the text.
Denotation of the related [meaning] does not occur all at once with every related term;
rather, it occurs according to the respective proximity of the related terms. (10)
The presentation of the distinction between the primary (prakṛti) and the modified (vikṛti):

"But in the case of the primary, because the meanings of the words are expressed by their own terms, the connection with the preceding [mantras] occurs first; the subsequent [connection] is for the sake of the postulated assistance—this is the further difference. (11)

The definition of extended application (atideśa) is as follows: the injunction follows along by means of transposition, by means of assistance, and by means of modified constituent elements as well as original ones; that is accepted as extended application.
When a procedure belongs to a particular location, its application extends elsewhere as well;
thus, the extension of both the type and the specific ritual properties is appropriate.
Just as a category found in one place is extended to another, so too are dharmas accepted; for them, there is the principle of extension (atideśa).
The objection regarding the lack of contradiction with the Tenth Book according to the view of a certain school:
"But in this way, a contradiction with the Tenth Book would follow for you. [Response:
"It is not so; that extension which is independent of a specific ritual purpose has been refuted. (15)

If the relation of the properties were to exist only through their being that [object], then cognition would not be established, because the mode [of the object] would be independent [of cognition]. // 26 //
Refutation of that [position]:
For when the relationship between ritual elements is understood in the archetype (prakṛti), a means—whether perceptible or imperceptible—is postulated for the sake of that relationship. (17)
When a relationship independent of any specific purpose has been understood in that same way, then—
whether it be a visible or an invisible means— it must be postulated even in the case of a modified sacrifice (vikṛti).
Therefore, a sublation based on the failure of the effect is not tenable, for even when the visible [means] is absent, an invisible means may indeed be possible. (19)
When dharmas enter into connection with a modification in dependence upon a specific purpose, then their sublation is established through the omission of that purpose. // 20 //
For since phenomena (dharmas), being endowed with their respective gateways, reach [their effects] by virtue of that effect,
there is at that time no occasion for the conceptualization of those gateways as separate entities.

If it is asserted that the relationship between properties is independent of their effects, then there would be no contradiction with the first chapter of the *Daśapāda*; however, that is not the case.

"Are the properties grasped as being identical with that [object], or is it rather its mode?"—this is the inquiry in the first section of the tenth book, for the purpose of establishing sublation. (24)

The presentation of the absence of contradiction with the tenth [book] and those following, according to his own view: And regarding that, the opponent says: "There is no possibility of defining the categories of things without the assistance provided by the [auxiliary] dharmas. (25)
Even though the injunction itself first requires a mode [of performance],
nevertheless, even in the case of the archetype (prakṛti), it does not [require it] by its own nature.
However, thorough comprehension occurs precisely according to the teachings as they have been heard;
therefore, his investigation is always preceded by the analysis of word-meanings. (27)

Therefore, because they have been previously cognized, the modified injunction attains its connection through the word-meanings alone; having grasped them, it [the injunction] itself [establishes the relation]. (28)
When the primary door is not obstructed, they ought not to obstruct that which provides assistance. // 29 //

The description of the tenets beginning with the tenth according to his own view: But the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin) says this: "It is true that dharmas precede [the self], and likewise..."
Even though they are not apprehended at that time, it is because of their lack of dependence [on other conditions]. // 30 //
For an injunction, moreover, requires a form that is yet to be accomplished;
it does not [require] already existing things, and thus it disregards even those things that have been perceived.
It has been shown that one first apprehends the relation by means of the mode itself, and subsequently [apprehends it] through the word-meanings as conceptualized by that mode. (32)
The removal of the doubt regarding the status of one set of phenomena as belonging to another set:
If it is asked, "How can phenomena belonging to one thing be joined with another?", this [objection] applies equally even in the case of assistance; thus it is said: // 33 //
"This statement—that there is no connection with the benefit—is laughable;
for if that [benefit] were not belonging to another, how then could it be extended [by analogy]? (34)
For in other cases, the extension of the nature of one thing to another body is indeed taught;
if it is argued that there is a contradiction in attaining that [other state] by becoming like it, no such contradiction exists. (35)

In the same way, for the sake of producing an entity, this is equally applicable to the categories of existence; yet there is this contradiction in cognition when one thing is joined with something belonging to another. (36)
In the Bhaṭṭa school’s view, there is no way for that [connection] to exist through another means;

thus, the presentation of the lack of logical consistency [is made]. However, those who do not accept a connection between the properties (dharmas) and the modified elements (vaikṛta) [are as follows]: 37.
In the case of the *apūrva*, the textual tradition regarding the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries is contradicted;
in the seventh and eighth [chapters], there is an investigation into their various modes of acquisition. (38)
For it is not logical that there should be deliberation regarding those six, since they are bound to the task;
if, however, the injunction itself is the task, then it too must be deliberated upon for that purpose.
Likewise, the deliberation of the fourth chapter would also apply here in this group of six;
thus, he demonstrates the logical justification according to his own view:
"For from the effect, the purpose of the instruction, the meaning of the injunction, and so forth, are understood. (40) 17.
Just as its status as being taught [by the Veda] has been explained, so too will its non-exclusion be stated. Therefore, having set aside the injunctive sense, another purpose is resorted to. (41)
This inquiry is established as the gateway to the sixfold set of tasks;
therefore, the extension [of principles] to the categories of meaning is considered here within this sixfold set. (42)
The assistance provided by that very same [initiation], which serves as the cause, is also shown in the statement:
"He initiates by means of the six," where the natural [mantras] are replaced by the modified ones. (43)
In this way, it would follow that there is an obstruction of those who lack limbs by means of those who possess them as limbs;
for they exist outside the state of being primary [limbs], merely for the sake of establishing assistance.
In that case, the archetypal [element] is not performed merely by virtue of being enjoined;
rather, this is accepted as an extension of the function (kāryātideśa) based on direct instruction (aupadeśika). // 45.18 //

The assumption that the assistance rendered in the archetype (prakṛti) is accomplished by means of the apūrva—on account of the meaning of the injunction as determined by the object of the instruction—is [the basis for this]. (46)
And for the person to be instructed, the presentation of the meaning of the word "instruction" according to his own view is agreed upon through the instruction of the elders;
for instruction is indeed [as follows].
Here, the composition of the text is being stated. // 47 //

And that [injunction] is established as a means of valid cognition with respect to its prescriptive meaning in the form of what is to be done; for whatever object is understood from it, that is not merely based on instruction.

That which an injunction implies for the sake of its own realization, and that which it is capable of postulating for the sake of the injunction’s fulfillment when it cannot otherwise reach completion—[all this is included within the injunction]. (49)
It is logical that [the Veda] is also derived from instruction, just like that which is understood through the literal words;
nor is it possible for an injunction to postulate a specific benefit [for one over the other]. (50)

For even though the archetypal [element] is capable of postulating a specific benefit, it does not do so for a specific modified object, just as the archetypal [element] does not [apply] to the modified. // 51 //
In that case, the reason why one accepts [the agency] of *prakṛti* alone is its simplicity;
for when there is a conflict between what is already established (*klṛpta*) and what must be postulated (*kalpya*), the acceptance of the established is the simpler course. (52)
This [connection] is established by means of the horse's statement, name, and gender, and it is brought into proximity;
however, the attainment of the distinction between the word-meanings would not occur without an auxiliary factor.

The specific distinction between the primary material cause (prakṛti) and its modifications (vikṛti) is stated; their attainment is through the effect, and their classification is through instruction. Furthermore, the assistance rendered to the primary material and the ritual items (padārtha) are also established through instruction. // 54 //
In the case of a modification, the properties are established through their function, and the specific manner is established through instruction.
This is the presentation of our own view:
even when this [rule] has been taught, the designation of it as an *atideśa* (extended application) is not precluded; for its meaning exists as a distinct location from its own original rule. (56)

The presentation of a fault in the Bhaṭṭa school’s doctrine that the direct injunction (*upadeśa*) and the extended application (*atideśa*) have distinct objects: "However, being directly enjoined and being extended by application are not contradictory for a single [element], for it is not accepted that the direct injunction and the extended application are [separate] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (57)

If both direct instruction (upadeśa) and extended application (atideśa) were indeed valid means of knowledge, then the description of the absence of previously mentioned defects in one's own system would result in a contradiction; however, this is not accepted here. (58)
Because it is to be known through that instruction, it is accepted as being "taught";
furthermore, since it exists elsewhere [in another form], "extended application" (atideśa) is also appropriate. // 59 //
The indication of the subject matter for both the instruction and the teaching according to his own system:
both sets of six rely upon the two means of valid cognition consisting of the instruction and its effect; they do not rely upon the primary rule (uddeśa) and its extension (atideśa). (60)

For if [the inquiry] were based on extension (atideśa), then in cases of sublation (bādha) and in the case of the common ritual framework (tantra), an investigation concerning the subject matter of what has been directly taught would not be possible at all. (61)

But since all [mental] reflections are established insofar as they have their activity based on the door [of the senses], it is logical here to consider that reflection is supported by its object. (62)
The suspicion that things (padārtha) are taught as being like auxiliaries [to an action]:
"But in this way, it would follow that things are taught [as ends in themselves];
for even by them, the meaning of the injunction is said to be expressed as conjoined with the effect. (Verse 63)
The refutation of that [objection] is stated:
In this way, there would be merely verbal [knowledge], not the status of being an object of authoritative instruction (upadeśa).
This distinction between the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is based on their respective modes of presentation. (64)
That which, being presented through direct instruction, attains connection with the meaning of the sentence is to be known as *aupadeśika* (based on instruction); and that is presented in two ways.
And [the meaning] presented by the text, as well as the meaning of the injunction presented [by it],
is like the benefit in the archetype, or like that which is not explicitly heard but must be enjoined.
That which is present in two ways as a mode is not truly present;
therefore, it is not based on instruction, but is merely bound by its effects.
Śālikanātha, striving to remove the delusion that serves as the foundation for previous treatises, has made this effort which bestows joy upon the learned. (68)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Course of Extended Application" (*atideśapārāyaṇa*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor (*mahāmahopādhyāya*) Śrīmacchālikanāthamiśra.
And this *Prakaraṇapañcikā* is completed.
